back: $|f(x)|$: reflect negative parts up. $f(|x|)$: reflect the $x \ge 0$ part in the y-axis.
Zeros of $f$ → vertical asymptotes; max ↔ min; points at $y = \pm1$ unchanged.
$|x| = x$ if $x \ge 0$ and $-x$ if $x < 0$ — the distance of $x$ from 0. Note $\sqrt{x^2} = |x|$.
Never below the $x$-axis; parts where $f < 0$ are reflected up; sharp corners where $f$ crosses the axis.
An even function: keep the part for $x \ge 0$ and reflect it in the $y$-axis (the left half of $f$ is discarded).
Same sign as $f$; large $|f|$ gives values near 0 (often a horizontal asymptote $y = 0$); a max of $f$ becomes a min of $\frac1f$ at the same $x$.
Never negative; zeros of $f$ become touching points; points with $f = \pm1$ map to $y = 1$; $|f| < 1$ shrinks, $|f| > 1$ grows.

front: (HL) How is $y = f(ax + b)$ obtained from $y = f(x)$?
back: $f\left(a\left(x + \frac ba\right)\right)$: horizontal stretch factor $\frac1a$, then translation $\frac ba$ left.

front: (HL) Why must you check solutions of $|A| = B$?
back: Splitting into $A = \pm B$ (or squaring) can produce values with $B < 0$, which cannot equal a modulus.
